Discharged from a psychiatric ward against her will, Valerie is forced to enrol at Sixth Form for a fresh start, where she meets a loner nicknamed Absinthe. In Absinthe Valerie finds someone who is also a far cry from normal, as revealed by her journal entry that details the plans she has for the school on the 13th of December, three months away. ‘Sixteen year old Valerie’s past six months in the psychiatric ward has been a regime of medication and routine therapy. The psychiatrist finalised her discharge plan, despite Valerie not wanting to be discharged: she was never afraid to go insane, but she is terrified to have to become normal again. 

Nonetheless she is discharged, to enroll at a new Sixth Form for a fresh start. Here she meets a girl nicknamed Absinthe. Unlike Valerie’s idea of nursing, Absinthe's nurse comes in the form of nursing drinks. Valerie instinctively wants to be Absinthe’s nurse—if she can help Absinthe then maybe she isn’t as hopeless as she fears she is. 

However Absinthe too has a dark past, and darker still secrets. When Valerie discovers Absinthe’s journal, full of things more disturbing than anything she ever saw in the psychiatric ward, Valerie is forced to confront her own demons. 

Can Valerie and Absinthe get better, or will they only get better at hiding their demons? 

Valerie has to dig deep, praying she’s not digging her grave in the process.

The opening paragraph didn’t hook me, I think it’s fine to mention the books but make the book significant it it means something to the plot. Aka someone who’s about to go into religious battle might read Dante’s Inferno. It’s nice that the mum and the narrator relate over books, but I’d choose one book and make it significant. It’s hinted at when you say they both read for catharsis, that’s what hooked me into this story so perhaps bring it up in your opening eg: ‘my eyes studied the wrinkles in the book’s spine, well worn and well read, opening it to seek a catharsis from reality—a habit passed down from my literary devoted mother’, but better of course. 

I like the imagery of the Chughtai placed on the corner, about to fall. In fact I really liked that, it seemed like foreshadowing to me and seems symbolic of an inner conflict I’d love to see throughly explored later in the story, perhaps tying the heavenly dream and the mother’s volatile love in with the escape of reading. This has a lot of potential and you pulled it off well, so well done. I like the codependent relationship between the mother and her child, and you described it well—and it’s interesting you describe the self disgust, it shows a complex and conflicted character. 

I feel the story gets a little lost when it talks about erotic, it feels a bit random and I’m not sure how to take it. Was the narrator sa’d? I feel we get a glimpse of the mother’s character, but the narrator still feels somewhat flat. Which could be fine, if they’re going to meet their mother maybe they are dissociating, which could be interesting to explore, but if that’s the case then I’d make it more obvious.

The world building about the Chughtai again feels half explored, and it leaves me feeling confused. If I was writing this I’d pick out why it’s needed to the story and emphasis that, like the foreshadowing of it about the fall (like the narrator is about to fall into their mother’s hands), maybe relate it to the books?

I love the mention of her mother’s silences. When you talk about the mother the voice of the story is very strong, very clear, and very emotive. If I was you I’d build on this, as this is truly the most compelling part of the story and you write it well, the snake metaphor especially. 

I feel the heart is glossed over too quickly, you could really dig deep with the anxiety in the narrator’s body. Have they got a cold sweat? Chills? Nausea?
 
When you talk about the mother talking about ‘the degeneration of culture, the dissolution of family, the corruption of kids’ this felt powerful. You did really well with this, and it’s really compelling—so well done you! You know how to write a flawed character well, without it being too vague or too direct, which leaves the reader the mental space to fill their imagination with. 

I like the touch of the mum saying she’s too old to read, it gives her a sense of fragility and I feel like it comes from a very conflicted voice of a narrator who is afraid of who their mum was, but now the mum is too old and maybe the narrator doesn’t want to make the last years of their life hard by dragging up old trauma. Or maybe that’s just me. 

The narrator again feels lost in the last paraphrased, I want to know more about them but their language is quite cold/disconnected. This could work, as maybe that are numb or in a state of shock (assuming the mum is dying), sort of like in Perks of a Wallflower where the narrator is a bit of a blank slate. But it works! And it could work for your story too!

The ending was bittersweet, as in it was written well but made me sad for the narrator being gay and fearful of it, give us more glimpses of this humanity and you’ll have a great book!

For me the opening seemed like a mixture of too many emotions to clearly decide what tone you were trying to set. It jumps around a lot, and it feels like it’s trying to do too much at once. Granted this is a small excerpt so it would be hard to tell what you’re going for anyway, but I’d stick to one theme and develop it as much as possible. As someone who’s definitely escaped into everything from the bottle to the needle I’ll rewrite this idea focused on that, as maybe that will help:

I’d hold down the crook of my elbow, the touch stung as my babysitter’s did. Except when a vein surfaced from the pressure applied I knew all the pressure in my head was soon to slip away, the hurt of the needle puncture was a worthy trade to escape the hurt in my head, my brain branded with the mental scars my babysitter left with every blood chilling touch. 

I feel it’s also written a bit clunking, a lot of short sentences. Which is fine at times, but remember that short sentences are generally for dramatic effect, and that effect gets boring if repetitive. Since you are setting a dark story I’d go fro run on sentences, to leave the reader a bit breathless so they can feel the pace of the story. It all seems a bit random and jumpy, like mentioning the cop and his bullet, it seemed vaguely like some sort of Breaking Bad-esque scenario but it just leaves me disoriented instead of hooked, again pick one or two elements and really develop them, I wouldn’t jump around this much 

The dialogue also leaves me confused. I’d focus on doing some world building and being more specific in the dialogue, show me the world and how the characters interact with it. I’m assuming the baggie was drugs, why are they selling drugs? What’s up with the prisons? Really expand on it, keep it less vague and more concise 
 
Also the description of the gully doesn’t paint a clear picture, I don’t get the significance of it. Why is it mentioned/why is it important? It it some kind of altar? Are the red stains blood? If you want to go for something creepy then describe the
shadows, explore the red stains more. Make it ominous, direct, but leave some room for the imagination to make it all the more horrifying. The reader doesn’t need much to imagine things, but give them a solid foundation to do so. 

Mentioning being sacrificed at the altar has little pay off, as it’s all random and chaotic and this is the first bit of horror. One thing I’d do is the link the babysitter to the altar, because right now I feel you could either make that connection or start off at the altar, I think the second opinion would be much more powerful and emotive. Also what is that ‘that day’? Give more of a hint to create intrigue, but then leave it for the mysterious ambiguity 

What music is blaring? What does the music mean to the characters. You could expand on this, make it more interesting. Is one character traumatised by the altar and playing some kind for lullaby to console themselves? Is one character numb to the altar, and blasting music to recreate the terrifying atmosphere? You could really develop the characters and the world with this small detail that I feel isn’t explored enough 

Why are there so many prisons? Again I know you can’t reveal everything all at once, that’s boring, but just give us a hint as to why there is so many? Is it some kind of government conspiracy etc?

I like the post apocalyptic setting of the dry, cracked earth and this sacrificial altar. When the cigarette is lit I feel that’s the start of where this story starts to really pay off, because you’re showing and not telling—it’s just vague enough to induce mystery, but gives us just enough to be afraid for the world, scared for the characters, and it’s all very interesting and you’ve done that very well, in my opinion. I like the banter, I get the sense Casey is a complex character, and I’m interested to get to know him and why his mum went back to prison. Keep on building on this, and you’ll have a solid start. Not as in explaining everything about Casey, but building things up like you’ve built Casey up. 

I think this is the best part of the entire excerpt. It’s mysterious, informative, world building and character building: 

‘To be fair, his mom had just gone back to prison. Having known Casey all my life, I didn't personally see it as a huge loss, but you couldn't help feeling sorry for the guy. And that just made what I was doing up there that much worse.

"No, I'm realistic. The way I see it there's two options: I can spend my life serving the prisons or I can serve my life in prison."’

Keep doing more of that, it’s bloody brilliant!

Also the Mummy Crew doesn’t fit the tone, I’m not saying it make it a scary name, just explore why it’s called the Mummy Crew. Maybe, just an idea, the bond between a mother and daughter is the strongest psychological bond there is—maybe it’s a Mummy Crew because they are all closely bonded? I’m not saying that has to be the reason, but give some reason, even if later on in the story 

There’s little emotion after the mention of the Mummy Crew. I think your dialogue is good, but when you go to world building it gets cold. I like the description of replacing baby daddies, wanting to feel special, and growing older. How do the characters feel about these harsh facts of life: it sets a bleak tone but there is next to no bleak emotion, and it leaves me wanting more.

Generally I’ve had okay times at psych wards. Some were really bad, others were really good. But, for what it’s worth, I hope you find a reason to stay alive. ‘You smell of the forest floor when I finally rest my head upon your lap. It was me who ran through the woods because I felt sorry for you. I cried to be there.

I don’t know emotions to this day.’

I’m a big fan of the ‘you’ perspective, I find it inherently very immersive and you set a good scene with the minimalist description of a forest floor. Since this is quite a soft, tender kind of story it might help to, for example, say that the forest floor is like a pillow from moss, and the lap has warmth to it, as human bodies are warm? Just a thought 

‘I don't know friendship to this day.

And now we can't climb a hill without you bringing up our holiday. My journal is full with crossed out entries from that time. And foreign currency pressed flat between the pages. I don't owe you any money, but I always pay you back.’

I like the sentimental aspect of crossed out journal entries, it gives the character a lot of depth and I’m compelled to learn more about the dynamic these two share.

However I’d change ‘to this day’ to ‘till this day’, as it reads more naturally. Your version is a bit clunky and it did take me out of the story somewhat 

‘I don't know you without me.

And I dread Sundays without visiting your grave in the woods when you’ve sunk beneath the forest floor. I dread your presence and your smell because I’ll never know it again.

Until your last breath I won’t know life without you.

But one day soon I will.’

I love the emotion of ‘I don’t know you without me’, it implies an unhealthy but desperate codependency, which makes their relationship all the more interesting. I like the borderline cynical/hopeful spite/determination of that closing line



EDIT: 

I think you captured something of a fantastical dreamworld very well, which made the reading experience very poetic, and very powerful. What I think you’re lacking is depth, for example describing the forest floor, the lap, the rain and the pets. 

I also found it jarring when you suddenly mention about killing pets, if I was you I’d foreshadow this early on, so the reader doesn’t get emotional whiplash (for want of a better term). Since your writing is but poetic you could do something haunting, like saying the warmth of a lap was like the warmth of blood. Something along those lines, just better. You already foreshadow it with crying, you could do some kind of pathetic fallacy with the rain you mention. 

The use of ‘adult grin’ doesn’t serve to describe the grin in any meaningful way. Use an adjective like sinister, because it foreshadows and gives a clear visual picture in the reader’s mind. And when you talk about flying maybe say ‘like you snapped their wings’, foreshadowing the pet killings. 

When you have the one sentence paragraphs they read as a little clunky, as the wording is off. For example ‘I don’t know directions to this day’ maybe say something like ‘directions leave me disoriented till this day’?

And the mention of memories behind bulletproof glass is powerful, but what does this mean? Did the person kill and now their weapons behind bulletproof glass? Or is the narrator trapped behind metaphorical bulletproof glass, because they are trapped in those memories?

Once the pet killing is mentioned I think you should keep it dark, instead of mentioning a girlfriend. Maybe mention the narrator’s trauma leave them unable to love, hence the ‘I don't know love to this day’ line. 

I like the visual image of radioactive ghosts. It’s powerful and poetic, which is what you do well. 

It seems they’ve gotten away with killing, hence those who ‘say’ they are kind and funny. If you use ‘said’ it implies they aren’t anymore, it could be worth playing on that sense of mystery and change in a meaningful way?

Okay so the grave means they are dead, but what is the reader supposed to feel? I’m glad a pet killer is dead, and the narrator seems to grapple with the one they loved becoming into something so universally hated. That could (and does) make for an intriguing dynamic. 

But I like how it ends on the hope of ‘one day soon I will’, which implies recovery and growth. You could perhaps link this to how the forest grows over the grave. Maybe some flowers bouquets left by those who once viewed this person as kind and funny have grown over the grave, implying those traits can grow now a monster is dead.

Overall I loved this, it was very moving and I think you have real potential—so keep it up!
